title: iPad mini 2026 rumors: Release date, OLED display, specs and price
content:
Macworld





For those who need a premium small-screen tablet, the iPad mini is a popular choice. But should you buy one now, or should you wait to see what Apple has in store for the next model? 
Most buyers should wait if they can. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple plans to announce the next iPad mini on October 27, with an OLED display and A20 Pro chip expected. 
Even more recent reporting points to an Apple media experience in Los Angeles on October 28. This experience doesn’t necessarily mean that Apple has moved the announcement back a day, it could allow journalists hands-on time with products announced on October 27. The iPad mini is among the rumored products, but it’s inclusion is unconfirmed.
Here’s what the latest rumors say about the release date, key upgrades, and whether it’s worth waiting. 
iPad mini 7 vs iPad mini 8 comparison


FeatureCurrent iPad miniNext iPad mini rumors

ReleaseOctober 2024October 27 announcement reported
ChipA17 ProA20 Pro expected
Display8.3-inch LCDOLED, possibly 8.5 inches
DesignCurrent designSimilar design, possibly slimmer bezels
Water resistanceNo official ratingImproved resistance rumoured
WirelessWi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread expected
Cellular modemQualcommApple C1X expected
Cameras12MP front and rear12MP rear and front cameras likely; landscape front-camera position expected
Apple IntelligenceSupportedSupported, with faster AI performance
PriceFrom $599 (was $499)Near $799 reported; unconfirmed.
Biggest upgrade—OLED display, faster chip and newer connectivity

 






2026 iPad mini release date: When will the new iPad mini launch?
Expected announcement: October 27, 2026, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple plans to announce the new iPad mini on October 27, alongside new Macs. 
Gurman had reported in July 2026 that Apple was targeting October for the OLED iPad mini release. Although a September report grouped the device among products expected in late 2026 or early 2027. The newer evidence points back toward an imminent launch.
In September, MacRumors saw a leak from “Apple’s own code,” that included references to the unreleased iPad mini, along with product imagery showing some of its new features. That report said the presence of these assets suggests the device is likely to launch soon and noted that Gurman expects the new iPad mini to arrive by the end of October.
That would fit Apple’s recent iPad mini schedule: the current A17 Pro model was announced in October 2024. However, Apple has not confirmed an event or release date, so an October launch should still be treated as an expectation rather than a certainty.


						

							


2026 iPad mini chip: Performance and specs 
A20 Pro chip expected
C1X modem expected on cellular models
N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread expected
The next iPad mini now looks likely to make a much bigger processor jump than previously expected. According to information discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors in September 2026, the new iPad mini is set to use the A20 Pro chip introduced with the iPhone 18 Pro.
That supersedes earlier evidence pointing to the A19 Pro. In August 2025, MacRumors reported that Apple code appeared to identify an A19 Pro-powered iPad mini, and that remained the leading expectation for much of 2026. The newer leak is more recent and specifically identifies the upcoming model with the A20 Pro, making that the strongest indication of Apple’s current plans. Apple has not officially announced the device, however, so its final specifications are not confirmed.
Moving from the A17 Pro to the A20 Pro would represent a major performance upgrade. The newer chip should bring substantially faster CPU and graphics performance, along with more capable on-device AI processing for Apple Intelligence, gaming, photo editing and other demanding workloads. It would also make the iPad mini unusually powerful for its size and narrow the performance gap with Apple’s larger iPads.
The current iPad mini has 8GB of RAM. Apple’s recent Pro-class iPhone chips have been paired with more memory, so the new model could receive an increase, but the September leak does not appear to confirm the iPad mini’s RAM allocation.
The processor may not be the only silicon upgrade. Apple is also expected to bring its N1 networking chip to the iPad mini, adding support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread. Cellular models are expected to adopt Apple’s C1X modem, replacing the Qualcomm modem used in the current generation.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Display
OLED display expected
Single-stack LTPS panel rumored
Apple has reportedly tested both 60Hz and 120Hz displays

				
					

				
			
The iPad Pro already uses OLED. The next iPad mini is also expected to adopt OLED, although reports point to a different panel technology.

Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




The biggest display upgrade expected for the next iPad mini is the move from LCD to OLED. Multiple reports, including those from Bloomberg and display-industry sources, have pointed to an OLED iPad mini arriving in 2026, and Samsung Display is reportedly already producing panels for the device.
OLED should bring deeper blacks, higher contrast, faster pixel response and improved viewing angles compared with the Liquid Retina LCD in the current iPad mini. Reports suggest that Samsung began mass production of OLED panels for the mini in June.
The exact screen size is less certain. Reports over the past two years have pointed to panels measuring between 8.4 and 8.7 inches, compared with 8.3 inches on the current model. A slightly larger display could be achieved through slimmer bezels without substantially increasing the size of the tablet, but the final panel dimensions have not been confirmed.
However, the iPad mini is not currently expected to receive the same display technology as the iPad Pro. Reports indicate that Apple will use a single-stack LTPS OLED panel, rather than the tandem OLED and LTPO technology used in the Pro models. That should keep costs lower, but the panel may not reach the same brightness levels as the iPad Pro display.
Earlier reporting pointed to a 60Hz display, but newer information leaves the refresh rate uncertain. In a October 15 Power On podcast, Mark Gurman claimed Apple has tested both 60Hz and 120Hz ProMotion displays for the next iPad mini. Gurman was unable to confirm which option Apple had selected.
An OLED display would improve contrast and black levels, but OLED does not guarantee ProMotion. 


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Design
Same overall size, with a slightly larger screen possible
More water-resistant design expected
New vibration-based speaker system

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPad mini has retained the same design since its major redesign in 2021, and the 2026 model is expected to keep that overall look. However, Apple could increase the display size slightly while maintaining the device’s current dimensions.
A newly spotted accessory listing offers another clue. MacRumors identified an iPad mini Smart Folio with model number A3632 on Apple’s French regulatory website. The number differs from existing iPad mini cases, suggesting a new accessory could be approaching. The regulatory filing doesn’t offer any clues about the dimensions of the new iPad mini, but does indicate some changes to the materials used in Apple’s iPad mini case. 
In December 2024, analysts at Display Supply Chain Consultants (DSCC) suggested in a supply chain analyst report that the next-generation iPad mini could feature an 8.5-inch display, up from the current model’s 8.3-inch panel. The report indicated that the chassis size would remain unchanged, meaning Apple could achieve the larger screen through slimmer bezels rather than a larger body.
Apple has now announced the iPhone Duo, whose 7.6-inch folding inner display brings it closer to small-tablet territory. However, its $1,999 starting price makes it a very different purchase from an iPad mini. The Duo goes on sale October 23.
Another rumor gaining traction is that the new iPad mini will be more water-resistant. That rumor comes from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who in October 2025 claimed Apple was developing a next-generation iPad mini with a significantly more water-resistant chassis. 
The more water-resistant design could involve changes to the speaker system as well as the chassis. Gurman previously reported that Apple was developing a vibration-based speaker that would allow it to eliminate some traditional speaker openings, reducing potential entry points for water.
Newly leaked Apple imagery, via MacRumors, appears to support that report. Images discovered in Apple’s code in September show a small groove cut into the top of the display glass, presumed to be for the speaker. MacRumors said the imagery appears to corroborate Gurman’s report of an all-new vibration-based speaker system.
It is not yet clear exactly how the new speaker system will work or how much additional water resistance it will provide. There is also no indication that Apple will give the iPad mini an official IP water-resistance rating.
There’s also a strong possibility of new color options. Apple currently offers the iPad mini in Blue, Purple, Starlight, and Space Gray, while the previous generation was available in Pink, Purple, Starlight, and Space Gray.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Cameras 
Landscape front camera expected
No major camera sensor upgrade currently rumored

				
					

				
			
No major camera-sensor upgrade has been reported, but the front camera is expected to move to the landscape edge.

Foundry




The clearest camera change for the next iPad mini appears to be placement rather than camera hardware.
Leaked imagery discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors in September 2026 shows the front-facing camera moved to the landscape edge of the display. That would bring the iPad mini into line with the rest of Apple’s current iPad lineup and should make video calls feel more natural when the tablet is used horizontally with a stand or keyboard.
The current iPad mini has a 12MP Wide rear camera and a 12MP Ultra Wide Center Stage front camera. So far, there have been no credible reports suggesting that Apple plans a major change to the resolution or camera sensors themselves.
Even if the camera hardware remains unchanged, the expected A20 Pro chip could still improve image processing and computational photography. However, there are currently no reports of new camera sensors, higher resolutions or additional lenses.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Price 
The iPad mini had held the same $499/£499 starting price since its 2021 redesign. That changed in June 2026, when Apple increased the entry-level price to $599/£599.
The OLED model could bring another substantial price increase. According to a Power On newsletter on October 11, the next iPad mini could start near $799 – around $200 more than the current model’s $599 starting price. 


						

							


Should I wait to buy a new iPad mini? 
Wait if: Your current tablet still meets your needs. With an announcement reportedly planned for October 27, it makes sense to see what Apple introduces before paying full price for the existing model. Announcement and shipping dates may differ. 
Buy the current model if: You need a small tablet immediately or find a substantial discount. Compare the saving with current retailer prices, and consider whether you would regret missing the expected OLED upgrade. 
Beware that waiting may be a disadvantage if Apple increases the price for the new model. In that case, buyers on a tighter budget may want to consider a substantially discounted current-generation iPad mini.

For many buyers, the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ or ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max is the better choice. They offer the same A20 Pro chip as the ‌iPhone Duo‌, a more versatile camera system, and a substantially lower price. Choose the Pro if you prefer a smaller, lighter phone, or pay $100 more for the Pro Max if you want a larger screen and longer battery life.

The camera system is the clearest reason to choose a Pro model. Its variable aperture adjusts automatically during everyday photography, while also giving photographers greater control over depth of field. The dedicated Telephoto camera provides much more flexibility for distant subjects, from performances and sporting events to travel photography. These advantages matter even if you never use professional capture formats.

Buyers who rely on ProRAW, ProRes, Apple Log 2, or the Pro models' full manual-control suite have an even stronger reason to choose an ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌. While the ‌iPhone Duo‌ does offer some manual camera controls, its selection of tools and formats is much more limited.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ is worth considering if you would regularly unfold it for reading, documents, viewing photos, watching video, or using two apps side by side. Think through a typical day and identify your specific tasks that would benefit from the inner display, such as keeping a reference document open while writing an email. ‌Apple Pencil‌ support could also make it useful for handwritten notes and annotations, but that support is coming later in 2026.

Being able to prop the phone up for a call or video, give someone a live preview while photographing them, or use StandBy away from a charger may be useful throughout the day. Buyers who want to experience Apple's first foldable may also value the novelty and flexibility of the design, even without a specific productivity need.

You still need to be comfortable with the changes to everyday features. ‌Touch ID‌ replaces ‌Face ID‌, and there is no Action button for a customizable shortcut. The outer front camera has a lower resolution than the Pro models' camera, while the inner camera is designed around ‌FaceTime‌ and lacks several photography features. If selfies or front-camera video are important to you, those differences deserve consideration alongside the rear cameras.

Apple Store should help establish whether its width, folded thickness, and weight suit the way you normally carry and use your phone.

Battery life also depends on how you use the two displays. Apple's U.S. figures put the ‌iPhone Duo‌ level with the smaller Pro for typical use, below the Pro Max. Its long outer-display video playback rating does not carry over to the inner display, so buyers planning to spend much of the day unfolded should pay particular attention to those separate figures.

The price gap remains significant at every storage tier. A 1TB ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max costs $100 less than the entry-level ‌iPhone Duo‌, which has 256GB of storage. At the same capacity, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ costs $700 more than the Pro Max or $800 more than the Pro. Buyers who need substantial local storage therefore have another reason to favor a Pro model.

inner-display repair fee is $999 without AppleCare+, compared with $329 for the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s display and $379 for the Pro Max's. Battery service costs $229, compared with $129 for either Pro model. A separate replacement of the inner display's cover layer is listed at $49 without coverage or $19 with ‌AppleCare‌+.

Standalone ‌AppleCare‌+ with Theft and Loss also costs more for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, at $19.99 per month in the United States rather than $14.99 for either Pro model. Buyers planning to insure their phone should include that recurring difference when comparing ownership costs.

Choose the ‌iPhone Duo‌ if its inner display would meaningfully improve the things you do on your phone, or if experiencing Apple's latest radical rethink of the iPhone is itself worth the premium and compromises to you. If you expect to spend most of your time on the outer display, the Pro models are easier to justify: You would otherwise be paying substantially more while making limited use of the feature that most distinguishes the ‌iPhone Duo‌.

title: Apple Store Down Ahead of iPhone Duo Pre-Orders
content:
Apple's online store is down ahead of iPhone Duo pre-orders, which begin at 5:00 a.m. Pacific Time on Friday, October 16.


"We love that early energy," reads the Apple Store's message when visiting the U.S. website. "Almost ready for you. Pre-order begins at 5:00 a.m. PT. See you soon." Apple has been opening pre-orders at 5:00 a.m. Pacific Time for several years, rather than the 12:01 a.m. start time it previously used.

title: No, Meta’s Muse will not run on your Mac
content:
Macworld





You may have seen the headlines by now. 
“Apple and Meta bury the hatchet — for AI“
“Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers“
“Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs“
“Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs“
None of these are exactly false, but you’d be forgiven for thinking that Meta’s popular new Muse agent will now run locally on your Mac. It will not. There’s a Muse app for Mac and iOS (and the web) but the actual agent itself and all the models it uses run on Meta’s servers in the cloud.
What these stories are referring to is the new open-weights model that Meta just released called Muse Spark Open, compared to Meta’s current generation of AI stuff, which is simply called “Muse.” Meta says Spark Open has the most capable open-weights model so far (from the U.S.). However, it’s not a competitor for the frontier closed models such as GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5; that would be Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, which are much bigger models that run only in the cloud.
Muse Spark is of the same generation, but it’s a smaller, lightweight, fast-response model made to be comparatively inexpensive. And yes, it will run natively on a Mac! Well, two Macs. But not your Macs.
Apple has a blog post about optimizing Muse Spark Open and two other models to run natively on Apple Silicon Macs. It’s interesting stuff, but it’s worth noting that the other two models (Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8) are the only ones that can run on a single Mac Studio. 
Muse Spark Open would require a whopping 1.6 terabytes of RAM in its native precision (BF16) just for the 800+ billion parameters alone. So Apple worked with Meta to optimize and tune it, and if you run it at a quantized 4-bit precision (NVFP4) you can get the memory requirement all the way down to… 493GB. That’s just for the model. There’s other overhead involved in actually running it and for macOS itself, so a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM can’t run it. I’ll remind you that the 512GB Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is not even out yet, and is expected to cost at least $15,000 and probably quite a bit more.
You need two Mac Studios with 512GB of RAM to run Muse Spark Open, connected via their Thunderbolt ports and running the new MLX framework for distributed computing over multiple Macs. You might get away with three Mac Studios with 256GB, Apple doesn’t say.
So yeah, you can run the latest open-weights model from Meta “right from your desk” as Apple says, provided your desk has over $30,000 of Mac Studio hardware on it.
No, you are not able to run the Muse agent locally on your Mac. You are not able to run the latest and best frontier LLM models from Meta (Muse Wonder) on your Mac. You can only run the latest and best open weights model on at least two very expensive and high-end Macs. For all but a small subset of researchers, you’d be much better off paying to run it on a cloud server.
If there’s a story here for regular consumers, it’s this: Apple is very serious about being the go-to hardware for AI researchers running local models, and that might potentially pay off in the form of well-optimized AI software meant for everyday people with Apple Silicon.

title: Best iPhone 2026: Every iPhone compared
content:
Macworld





Apple’s 2026 iPhone lineup is broader than ever, ranging from the relatively affordable iPhone 17e to the high-end iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus the ultra-thin iPhone Air and the new folding iPhone Duo. That gives buyers more choice, but it also makes picking the right model more complicated than simply choosing the newest or most expensive iPhone.
For most people, the iPhone 17 is the best all-round choice, thanks to its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, strong battery life, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. The iPhone 17e is the better option if price matters most, while the iPhone 18 Pro is the model to choose for the best cameras and performance. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds the longest battery life, the iPhone Air prioritises thinness and low weight, and the iPhone Duo offers Apple’s biggest and most flexible display.
Which iPhone is best for you will therefore depend on what you value most. Camera enthusiasts should look closely at the Pro models, heavy users may prefer the Pro Max for its battery life, while parents, older users and anyone trying to keep costs down may find the 17e a much better fit. There can also be excellent value in buying a discounted or refurbished older iPhone rather than paying full price for the latest hardware.
This guide focuses on the best iPhone to buy for different types of user and budget. If you want to dig deeper into the differences between every model, see our complete iPhone Buying Guide, where we compare the cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Buy iPhone 17 if
Buy the iPhone 17 if you want the best all-round iPhone without paying Pro prices. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, excellent cameras, strong battery life and 256GB starting storage make it particularly appealing to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 14 or older.
Don’t buy iPhone 17 if
Don’t buy it if you want optical zoom beyond 2x or Apple’s most advanced camera features—in that case, choose the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Air is a better choice if thinness and low weight are your priorities, while existing iPhone 16 owners may find the upgrade relatively modest unless ProMotion and improved battery life are particularly important.

For the extra $200, the iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, Dynamic Island, a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera with macro photography, a brighter screen, stronger graphics performance, a better 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera and longer battery life. For most people who can afford the difference, it’s money well spent.
What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 16?
For $100 more, you get double the base storage at 256GB, a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, an upgraded 48MP Ultra Wide camera, an improved 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, longer battery life, faster charging and the newer A19 processor. At full price, the iPhone 17 is the better buy.

What do you miss compared with the iPhone 17?
The iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, newer A19 processor, upgraded 48MP Ultra Wide camera, improved 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, longer battery life and 256GB of storage as standard. Unless the iPhone 16 is heavily discounted, the 17 is easily worth the difference.
Key specs
The iPhone 16 combines the A18 chip with a 48MP Fusion Main camera, 12MP Ultra Wide camera, Camera Control, the Action button and Apple Intelligence support. It remains a capable smartphone, but its 128GB starting storage and older display make it less compelling than the newer iPhone 17e and iPhone 17.
Starts at: $699 / £699
Display: 6.1-inch Super Retina XDR OLED
Chip: A18
Storage: 128GB–512GB
Cameras: 48MP Main + 12MP Ultra Wide
Battery: Up to 22 hours of video playback
Should you buy or wait?
Don’t buy at full price. Only consider the iPhone 16 if it’s heavily discounted below the iPhone 17e; otherwise, Apple’s newer models offer substantially better value.

							
		


Which iPhone has the best camera? iPhone 18 Pro

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both models use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.
The headline upgrade is the 48MP Main camera with variable aperture, which gives photographers more control over depth of field and should improve low-light performance. The Pro models also include a 48MP Ultra Wide camera and a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, giving them far more flexibility than Apple’s cheaper iPhones.
The standard iPhone 17 is still an excellent camera phone, with 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras, plus an improved 18MP Centre Stage front camera. For everyday photography it will be more than enough for most people, but it lacks the dedicated telephoto lens, longer zoom and advanced video features of the Pro models.
The iPhone Duo is more compromised. Despite its premium price, it has only two 48MP rear cameras and lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and Apple Log. Its strengths are instead its fold-specific shooting features and dual-screen flexibility.
The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile, with just a single 48MP rear camera.
Our choice: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It offers the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.


						

							


Which iPhone has the best battery life? iPhone 18 Pro Max

				
					

				
			
Bigger iPhone means bigger battery.

Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback. That puts it comfortably ahead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro and makes battery life one of the strongest reasons to choose the Pro Max.
The iPhone Duo comes surprisingly close, with up to 44 hours of video playback when using its outer 5.4-inch display. However, battery life drops to around 31 hours when using the larger 7.6-inch folding display, so the Pro Max remains the better choice if endurance is your priority.
The iPhone 18 Pro is also excellent, offering up to 36 hours of video playback. That makes it a good compromise if you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max.
Further down the range, the iPhone 17 offers up to 30 hours, making it the best mainstream option for battery life. The iPhone Air manages around 27 hours despite its exceptionally thin design, while the iPhone 17e reaches 26 hours.
The older iPhone 16 trails the current lineup at up to 22 hours of video playback.
Our choice: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear winner. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travellers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.


						

							




Here’s how the current iPhone lineup compares in terms of battery life

iPhone 18 Pro MaxUp to 43 hoursTBC~15 min (60W+)
iPhone DuoUp to 44 hours outer / 31 hours innerTBC~20 min (60W+)

iPhone AirUp to 27 hours880~30 min (20W)

What is the best value iPhone? iPhone 17

				
					

				
			
Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry




The iPhone 17 offers the best overall value for money in Apple’s current lineup. The iPhone 17e is cheaper, but the extra $200/£200 for the iPhone 17 buys a surprisingly large number of worthwhile upgrades.
You get a larger 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Always-On support and Dynamic Island, rather than the 17e’s standard 60Hz 6.1-inch screen. The iPhone 17 also adds a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera, including macro photography, along with a better 18MP Centre Stage front camera.
Battery life is stronger too, at up to 30 hours of video playback, compared with 26 hours on the iPhone 17e. You also get stronger graphics performance and a more premium overall experience, while both phones start with a generous 256GB of storage.
At $799/£799, the iPhone 17 also compares very favourably with the older iPhone 16. For just $100/£100 more, you get double the base storage, ProMotion, a larger and brighter display, improved cameras, the newer A19 chip and significantly better battery life.
If your priority is spending as little as possible, choose the iPhone 17e which delivers excellent performance for $599/£599. Or seek out a refurbished iPhone from the Apple Refurbished Store or another place that sells refurbished iPhones.
Our choice: In terms of the features and hardware you get for every pound or dollar spent, the iPhone 17 is the sweet spot. For most buyers, it delivers the best balance of price, performance, cameras, display quality, battery life and longevity without paying for Pro-level features they may never use. Even better if you can find a iPhone 17 deal, then you are really getting a bargain. 


						

							


Best iPhone for gaming: iPhone 18 Pro

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro is the best iPhone for gaming for most people, thanks to its combination of the A20 Pro chip, seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling.
The A20 Pro is Apple’s fastest iPhone processor, but the cooling system is just as important for gaming. Better heat management should help the iPhone 18 Pro maintain high performance for longer during demanding games, rather than slowing down as the phone gets hot. Its 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display also provides smooth animation and responsive gameplay without making the phone excessively large or heavy.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers essentially the same gaming performance, but adds a much larger 6.9-inch display and significantly longer battery life. That arguably makes it the best choice for serious mobile gamers who value screen size and endurance, although it is heavier and costs more.
The iPhone Duo also uses the A20 Pro and has an enormous 7.6-inch folding display, which could be fantastic for some games, but its weight, price and unconventional form factor make it a more specialised choice.
Our choice: For most gamers, the iPhone 18 Pro offers the best balance of performance, cooling, display quality and portability. It’s the best choice if you prefer a more pocketable device but still want top-tier gaming power.


						

							


Best iPhone for seniors and older users: iPhone 17e

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




For most older users, the iPhone 17e is probably the best choice, because it combines a relatively simple feature set with modern performance, strong battery life and a lower price than Apple’s flagship models.
Its 6.1-inch OLED display is large enough to make text, icons and controls easy to see without making the phone too bulky, while the A19 chip should keep it feeling fast for years. It also supports Apple Intelligence and starts with 256GB of storage, so there’s plenty of room for photos, apps and videos.
The iPhone 17 is a better option for someone who would benefit from a larger and more advanced display. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion screen, Always-On support and higher brightness can make scrolling, reading and outdoor use more comfortable. It also offers stronger battery life and better cameras, although it costs more.
We don’t recommend the iPhone Air, Pro Max or Duo for older users. The Air sacrifices battery life and camera flexibility for thinness, while the Pro Max and Duo are much heavier and considerably more expensive.
Our choice: iPhone 17e is the perfect choice for most older users.


						

							


Best iPhone for kids: iPhone 17e

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




The iPhone 17e is the best iPhone for most children. As Apple’s most affordable current-generation model, it offers the best balance of price, performance and longevity, while being easier to justify than a flagship model if it gets lost or damaged.
It uses the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17, albeit with one fewer GPU core, so it’s easily fast enough for games, social media, schoolwork and Apple Intelligence. Battery life is strong, the 6.1-inch OLED display is a sensible size for smaller hands, and the 48MP camera is more than capable for everyday photos, even though it lacks an Ultra Wide lens.
The iPhone 17 is the better choice for older teenagers who care more about photography, video or display quality. It adds a 48MP Ultra Wide camera, a better front camera and a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion display, but costs considerably more.
A hand-me-down iPhone is also worth considering. It’s the cheapest option and better for the environment, provided you erase the phone first, create a Child Account through Family Sharing, and configure Screen Time and parental controls before handing it over. Read: How to set up an iPhone for a child. 
Whichever iPhone you choose, those controls matter. In iOS 27, Apple is expanding Screen Time with new category-based Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, more flexible app schedules and improved contact controls. Communication Safety can also detect and blur sensitive, violent or graphic content.
For very young children, an iPad may still be a better first Apple device. By the time they reach 11 or 12 though, an iPhone becomes much more useful for staying in touch.
Our choice: iPhone 17e for most kids; iPhone 17 for older teens who want better cameras and display quality.


						

							


Should you buy an older iPhone? 

				
					

				
			
Macwelt




Buying an older iPhone can be a great way to save money, but the key is choosing a model that still has plenty of useful life ahead of it. Apple typically provides around five to seven years of major iOS updates, with security updates often continuing for longer, so a relatively recent iPhone can remain perfectly usable for years.
We wouldn’t recommend simply buying the cheapest iPhone you can find. Very old models may technically run recent versions of iOS, but performance, battery condition and access to newer features can become increasingly compromised. We currently recommend avoiding anything older than the iPhone 15 Pro because even the iPhone 15 doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. You should definitely avoid models such as the iPhone XS and XR that can no longer run the latest iOS releases.
A refurbished recent-generation iPhone can offer particularly good value. You may be able to buy a former Pro model with better cameras and displays for less than a new entry-level iPhone. Buying from a reputable refurbisher is important, however: check the warranty, battery condition, returns policy and whether genuine replacement parts have been used. Apple’s own refurbished iPhones include a new battery and outer shell and come with a one-year warranty.
Our advice: A discounted or refurbished iPhone 16 or newer should offer an excellent combination of price, features and longevity.

title: Meta and Apple Bring Muse Spark Open AI Model to Mac Studio
content:
Meta today announced the release of Muse Spark Open, which it says is the "most capable U.S. open-weight model to date."


‌Meta‌ worked with Apple to bring Muse Spark Open to the Mac, and the model can run on a desktop setup with two 512GB Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios running the latest MLX framework. ‌Meta‌ CEO Mark Zuckerberg thanked Apple CEO John Ternus for working with Meta.


@finkd Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!
— John Ternus (@johnternus) October 15, 2026



Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters with 42 billion active parameters and a 1 million-token context window. It is meant for coding and agentic work, and ‌Meta‌ says it excels at extended tasks, multi-step reasoning, and software engineering.

Mac Studio, and ‌Meta‌ says the ‌Mac Studio‌ paired with Muse Spark Open is the "best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop." From ‌Meta‌:
Apple's unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

Apple hasn't released the 512GB ‌Mac Studio‌ as of yet, but it's supposed to be coming later this month. It won't be cheap, because the 256GB ‌Mac Studio‌ is already priced over $10,000.

The model is available through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter, and Together AI, with model weights downloadable from Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. Muse Spark Open is free to download and has a license allowing limited commercial use.

title: Safari is getting ready for Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook
content:
Macworld





The touchscreen MacBook is reportedly going to be a reality very soon (October 28, apparently), and one of the questions about the new way to interface with the Mac is how macOS will accommodate our fingers. According to some clues in the latest beta, we can get an idea of what Apple is planning.
A post by itspdfu points out that Safari in the macOS beta has new UI elements designed for touch input. When rearranging tabs, the tab “lifts” and then enlarges as you drag it to the new location, then goes back to its original size when you drop it. Tabs don’t currently operate like this when you click and drag using a mouse or trackpad.


macOS 27 changes to accommodate touch, part 1: 
Safari
•  Tabs lift and scale as you drag to reorder.
•  Tap and hold a tab to open its context menu. The touch menu omits “Ask Siri.”
Added in 27.2 beta 3 & 4. pic.twitter.com/KfHnL1Guxe
— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 14, 2026





Also, you can tap and hold a tab to open the context menu, but it doesn’t show an Ask Siri option as it does with a mouse or trackpad–I’m not sure why Apple removed it. It’s also hard to tell from the screen capture whether the contextual menu options are slightly larger to make them easier to tap. 
But it’s clear that Apple is rethinking how we interact with macOS ahead of a big interface chance. We expect the new MacBook will ship with macOS 27.2 preinstalled when it arrives.
Itsdpfu, who has a reputation of accurate leaks, also said their post is “part 1” so stay tuned for more.
creator: Macworld

title: Apple's 'Minions' research turns idle Mac GPUs into a virtual GPU cloud
content:

The theory is a simple one. Macs have powerful GPUs that spend most of their time idle, especially during everyday computing tasks.

title: Apple TV 4K 2022 vs. 2026 Buyer's Guide: All Differences Compared
content:
Apple announced the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K earlier this week, introducing the A19 chip, built-in microphones for hands-free Siri, four-speaker HomePod surround sound, and an updated ‌Siri‌ Remote. It replaces the third-generation model introduced in 2022, bringing a number of internal changes while retaining the same basic design and most of the same entertainment features.


The new model costs $299 and comes with 128GB of storage. ‌Siri‌ AI is also coming to the third-generation model, and the new remote can be purchased separately for existing devices. Apple says the assistant will be available in beta with tvOS 27.2 on second-generation and later ‌Apple TV‌ 4K models, including conversational entertainment searches, follow-up questions, and personal context through a compatible paired device.

The new model's distinctive hardware benefit is direct voice input through the box's microphones; access to the voice assistant itself is shared. Whether you should upgrade therefore comes down to which hardware changes you will actually use.

Configurations, Connectivity, and Price

The differences in configurations, connectivity, and pricing between the third- and fourth-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are as follows:



‌Apple TV‌ 4K (3rd Generation)
‌Apple TV‌ 4K (4th Generation)


64GB model: Wi-Fi only
128GB model: Wi-Fi and Ethernet
Single 128GB configuration with Wi-Fi and Ethernet


Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax)
Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be)


Bluetooth 5.0
Bluetooth 6


Gigabit Ethernet on the 128GB model only
Gigabit Ethernet as standard


Thread networking on the 128GB model only
Thread networking as standard


Original U.S. launch prices: $129 for 64GB; $149 for 128GB
U.S. launch price: $299 for 128GB


Final prices before replacement: $199 for 64GB; $249 for 128GB
$299 for 128GB


Now discontinued
Available to pre-order


Released November 4, 2022
Available November 13, 2026




raised the older model's prices in June 2026, so comparing the new model exclusively with its predecessor's original launch pricing misses an intervening increase. Against the final price of the equivalent 128GB model, the new ‌Apple TV‌ costs $50 more. Against the previous entry-level configuration, it costs $100 more and includes twice the storage, Ethernet, and Thread connectivity. 

A15 Bionic vs. A19

The A19 chip brings a substantially newer chip architecture to the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple says the fourth-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K delivers the following improvements over the third-generation model:


Up to 50% faster CPU performance.

Up to twice the GPU performance.



The table below lists capabilities of two chip architectures. 



A15 Bionic Chip
A19 Chip


Made with TSMC's 5nm (N5P) process
Made with TSMC's third-generation 3nm (N3P) process



Dynamic Caching


Software-based ray tracing
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing


Mesh shading without the newer dedicated hardware acceleration
Hardware-accelerated mesh shading



Dedicated Neural Accelerators in each GPU core


16-core Neural Engine
Updated 16-core Neural Engine architecture


Display engine and image signal processor
Updated display engine and image signal processor



Dedicated AV1 hardware decoder


Up to 4x multisample anti-aliasing
Up to 8x multisample anti-aliasing


Maximum 1D, 2D, and cube-map texture dimensions of 16,384 pixels
Maximum 1D, 2D, and cube-map texture dimensions of 32,768 pixels



Universal texture compression



MetalFX denoised upscaling capability



Depth bounds testing




GPU Neural Accelerators supply dedicated hardware for machine learning calculations. 

While GPU improvements will be particularly useful for gaming, it is unclear just how much the full breadth of the chip architecture improvements will make a meaningful difference to the ‌Apple TV‌.

Hands-Free Siri and HomePod Audio

The new microphones and expanded ‌HomePod‌ support provide some of the clearest functional differences between the two devices:



‌Apple TV‌ 4K (3rd Generation)
‌Apple TV‌ 4K (4th Generation)


No built-in microphone array in the box; microphone only in the ‌Siri‌ Remote
Three built-in far-field microphones with voice isolation, alongside the microphone in the ‌Siri‌ Remote


‌Siri‌ voice input through the remote or another compatible device
Direct hands-free activation using "‌Siri‌" or "Hey ‌Siri‌," with echo cancellation while audio is playing


‌HomePod‌ TV audio through a single speaker or stereo pair
Four-speaker ‌HomePod‌ surround sound using matching front and rear pairs



Automatic positioning, timing, and level calibration for the four-speaker setup



Whole Room Audio mode distributes sound across four ‌HomePod‌ speakers




HomePod mini 2 or second-generation full-sized ‌HomePod‌ speakers. You can use four matching speakers or combine two matching front speakers with a different matching rear pair. For example, two full-sized HomePods can serve as the front speakers and two ‌HomePod mini 2‌ units as the rear speakers.

First-generation full-sized HomePods and original ‌HomePod‌ mini speakers are excluded from this new four-speaker configuration. Existing owners should account for any speaker replacements or additions when considering the cost of upgrading.

Whole Room Audio serves a different purpose from directional home theater sound, distributing audio more evenly around the room for music, sports, and more.

Hands-free ‌Siri‌ support also has its own language requirements. Apple lists Mandarin Chinese, Dutch, English, Finnish, French, German, Hebrew, Norwegian, and Swedish, subject to regional availability. 

Siri Remote Differences

The fourth-generation ‌Siri‌ Remote retains the familiar design and controls while making a misplaced remote easier to find:



‌Siri‌ Remote (3rd Generation)
‌Siri‌ Remote (4th Generation)


Bluetooth 5.0
Bluetooth 6


Nearby finding through iPhone, with proximity guidance
Find My with Precision Finding on a compatible iPhone



Bluetooth Channel Sounding for precise location tracking



Built-in speaker for playing a sound to locate the remote


66 grams
69.6 grams




The older remote already supported nearby finding with an iPhone. The new remote's additional benefits are precise location guidance and an audible alert. Precision Finding uses Bluetooth Channel Sounding, providing precise tracking without requiring a UWB chip.

iPhone 17 or later, excluding the iPhone 17e, or an iPhone Air or iPhone Duo running the latest software. You can also ask ‌Siri‌ to find the remote through the ‌Apple TV‌'s built-in microphones and have the remote play a sound.

available separately for $59 and works with the third-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, every earlier ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, and even the ‌Apple TV‌ HD. 

Design, Dimensions, and Weight

Both generations retain the compact black enclosure and Apple logo. The principal visible changes are the microphone hardware and the repositioned front light.




‌Apple TV‌ 4K (3rd Generation)
‌Apple TV‌ 4K (4th Generation)


Width
93 mm
93.24 mm


Depth
93 mm
93.24 mm


Weight
Wi-Fi: 208g
Wi-Fi + Ethernet: 214g
217g


Status light
Positioned toward the right
Positioned in the center


Packaging
At least 90% fiber-based packaging
100% fiber-based packaging




The new box weighs three grams more than the previous Ethernet model and nine grams more than the Wi-Fi-only model. The centered front light also indicates when the built-in microphones are listening for commands.

Should You Upgrade From the Third-Generation Apple TV 4K?

Most third-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K owners should keep their existing device. For ordinary streaming through television speakers, a soundbar, or an AV receiver, the new model does not add new capabilities. The maximum viewing resolution and HDR support remains the same. ‌Siri‌ AI's availability on the older hardware further reduces the need to replace a working device.

The strongest reason to upgrade is a planned four-speaker ‌HomePod‌ system. If you already own two second-generation full-sized HomePods and want dedicated rear speakers, the new ‌Apple TV‌ enables a specific setup your existing model cannot provide. Include the cost of additional or replacement speakers when judging the upgrade.

Hands-free control is another practical reason if you regularly use ‌Siri‌ and want to speak directly to the device. It is likely to be more useful when the ‌Apple TV‌ is directly in the viewing room than when it is installed in a separate equipment cupboard or rack.

AV1 hardware decoding may justify the upgrade for a particular media library or playback workflow. Gaming enthusiasts may also value the newer GPU architecture, but the benefit depends on the games available for tvOS and how developers use the hardware. 

If locating the remote is a source of frustration, buying the $59 ‌Siri‌ Remote separately costs $240 less than replacing the entire ‌Apple TV‌. That purchase supplies the new remote features while retaining your existing device.

Should You Buy the Third- or Fourth-Generation Model?

For a new purchase, the fourth-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is the stronger choice when the price difference is modest or you intend to use its exclusive features. Compared with the older 128GB model's final $249 Apple price, the $50 premium is easier to justify than the much larger difference suggested by comparing original launch prices.

That being said, a discounted third-generation model remains a sensible purchase. The older model is particularly appealing when the saving is substantial and you are not interested in a four-speaker ‌HomePod‌ sound system.

title: Greg Joswiak Says Apple Isn't Focused on Making AI for 'Lunatic Fringe'
content:
In an interview with TIME's Andrew R. Chow, Apple's marketing chief Greg Joswiak said Apple Intelligence is meant for "everyday people" as opposed to the "lunatic fringe."


The full sentence: "In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley's 'lunatic fringe,' as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it."

Joswiak apparently believes Apple Intelligence is not for "die-hard AI believers chasing superintelligence," as Chow described it.

"We love them, and they can use it too, but that's not our target," said Joswiak. "It's how to make it better for everyday people."

title: HomeView quickly won a place in my heart—and my home
content:
Macworld





Apple has taken its sweet time to make a smart display – just as it didn’t rush to make a folding phone. Google and Amazon have been in the smart display business for the best part of a decade, while Apple fans have been watching from the sidelines, with a HomePod in the corner of their kitchen and an iPad propped against the toaster. 
I’ll admit that when I first heard the rumours about Apple’s smart display, I expected the final product to look like an original HomePod speaker with a screen bolted on. But within a few minutes of seeing HomeView at Apple’s Home event in New York, I was smiling. It’s a charming little device that’s both a household device and a personalized one, something you can’t say about the single-user iPad. There are a couple of things to note about HomeView, which I’ll get to, but there’s a lot to love.
Cute and compact
HomeView is cute. That might not be the most eloquent adjective, but it’s the best way to describe how I felt when seeing it for the first time. A 7-inch LCD screen floats above a rounded aluminium base on a stainless-steel hinge, and you can nudge the display back or forward depending on whether it’s on a low nightstand or a tall counter. 
The hinge is a joy, too. It has firm, satisfying resistance, so the screen moves when you want it to and stays put when you let go – not too dissimilar to how I felt about the iPhone Duo when I tried it last month. It feels high-end in the way Apple hardware usually does, with no creaking, no plastic pretending to be metal, and a premium, solid feel all over.

				
					

				
			
HomeView’s low-profile design will look great on a table or a countertop.

Foundry




There are four color options—Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray—and Apple matches the USB-C cable to the body, similar to the iMac and its accessories. They’re muted shades that will blend well with whatever’s around it: wood, tile, or painted walls. Starlight was my favorite of the four, with its warm, soft tone, but they’re all lovely. 
The device itself includes a several rows of holes on the base and under the display for speakers, which pack two full-range drivers into the display, plus a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators in the base. It looks more like a Dyson appliance than an Apple gadget, but it sounds great for something so compact. Think somewhere between a HomePod mini and the full-size HomePod: noticeably fuller and punchier than the mini, without quite the room-filling presence of its big sibling.
If you’d rather put a HomeView in a hallway or on the kitchen wall, there’s a wall-mounted version too, which is only available in Silver or Space Gray. That model has the same aluminium display frame, but without the speaker base, the sound quality won’t be as good, so that’s something to consider.
Shared yet personalized
HomeView can do a lot, but the feature I appreciated most was face recognition. HomeView can learn up to six faces within a household, and once it recognises you, a swipe up from the bottom of the screen brings up a home screen that is not only familiar but personalised, too. 
Your calendar, reminders, messages and widgets will all appear, along with the design customisations you’ve made, such as coloured or clear app icons. If someone else comes into the frame, HomeView will ask whether you want to switch profiles, and if you do, their home screen will then appear seamlessly. 

				
					

				
			
HomeView can be a personal device if you’re signed into an Apple Account.

Foundry




It’s a smart way to work around the problem with shared screens. A kitchen display is a family device, but it’s helpful to have personal content, and HomeView manages to be both. It is worth noting that to show personal information like calendars and messages, the person not only needs to be recognised, but their iPhone also needs to be close by and “recently” unlocked.
Handoff was also impressive, and it’s another area where being an Apple household will really pay off. In my demo, an iPhone was held next to the HomeView screen with a recipe open in Safari, and it carried over to HomeView without hesitation. FaceTime calls jump across the same way, as does media, so it looks like it will be lovely and simple to start something on your iPhone and move it over to the bigger HomeView display.
Jumping back to recipes for a second, though, as this was a standout feature and a good indication of how Apple expects it will be used. Open a recipe in Safari on the HomeView display (or hand one off from your iPhone), and it will automatically pull out the ingredients and instructions. Tap “Start Cooking,” and HomeView will then present you with a single step at a time, allowing you to swipe through to the next when ready. 
It handles timers well, too, picking out the cooking times buried in each step and starting a timer immediately if you tap on it. You can set multiple timers, and they appear at the top of the HomeView display. It works much like Dynamic Island, though tapping it expands the timer to the full screen rather than an expanded view like on the iPhone.

				
					

				
			
There are few apps on HomeView, but you won’t use it like an iPhone.

Foundry




At the heart of HomeView is Apple’s new Siri AI, which can finally hold a conversation, follow up on previous queries, and answer questions that would previously have earned a shrug from the old Siri. With an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone paired, Siri AI can dig into your calendar and messages to use personal context to find things for you, too. 
I saw it in a demo, and it worked well (as demos usually do). There’s reason to be optimistic, though—I’ve been impressed with Siri AI over the last few months, and I expect it to be just as good on HomeView.
Guests aren’t left out either, but if your visitors have an Android phone, the experience won’t be anywhere near as rich or polished as those baked into the Apple ecosystem (no surprises there). Anyone without an Apple Account can still use HomeView, and the owner can select what they get access to in guest mode, such as playing music, browsing shared photos, or turning on the lights, while keeping everyone’s personal stuff locked away. There’s also a feature that uses the front camera to show you what you look like, in case you don’t feel like looking in a mirror. 
A couple of considerations
There are a couple of elements that take some of the shine off, though. HomeView works with accessories that support Apple Home or Matter, including Apple’s new Home Collection of cameras, thermostats, and a lock. That’s a lot of newer smart home products, but it’s far from everything. Many popular smart home brands, such as Ring, don’t support either, and if your setup leans on them, HomeView’s dashboard may end up with a few gaps where your gear should be.

				
					

				
			
HomeView is great for photos and FaceTime calls, but you won’t be using it much to watch movies.

Foundry




Apple would clearly love you to build your home around its ecosystem from day one, and that’s fine if you’re starting fresh. If you’ve spent years piecing together a mixed setup, though, HomeView leaves you with two options: live with the gaps or start replacing things. For example, the Home Camera face can stream up to nine camera feeds at once, which is great, but only if your cameras make the cut. If you’re considering the HomeView primarily as a smart home hub, my advice would be to check what you already own against Apple’s compatibility list before you pre-order.
The built-in camera has its own limits, too. It’s a 12MP sensor with Center Stage, so it does a great job of keeping you in frame on FaceTime, even as you shuffle around the kitchen. Unlike Google’s Nest Hub Max, though, it can’t act as a security camera or allow you to “Drop In” on your home, as you can with Amazon’s Echo Show devices. HomeView can work as an intercom, but it doesn’t offer anything with video like either of those.

				
					

				
			
HomeView can show live camera views, but only if you have the right accessories.

Foundry




Finally, while the lovely square screen has plenty going for it, it isn’t going to be great for watching video. The shape makes it stand out from rivals, and it suits album art, photos, and recipes perfectly, but it works against watching a quick TV show or recipe on YouTube while cooking. Instead, you’ll get thick bars above and below, which would be bearable for keeping an eye on a game while you cook, but if you want to actually watch something properly in the kitchen, propping that iPad back up against the toaster will do a much better job.
Last but not least, there’s no physical privacy switch. Apple processes camera and microphone data within the A18’s Secure Enclave, which neither the software nor Apple can access, according to the company. However, some users will likely still want a way to shut off the camera and microphones physically, as competitors offer, rather than relying solely on software toggles. 
Is HomeView worth a $299 pre-order?
Apple HomeView costs $299, with the wall-mounted model priced the same. The catch with the wall version is that the mounts are sold separately, starting at $59.95 for the USB-C plug-in option, $79.95 for the AC-wired option, and $129.95 for a Power over Ethernet mount that will arrive in early 2027. Hanging one in your hallway, then, costs closer to $360 or more, plus any additional costs for installation. And for some reason, it doesn’t come with a power adapter like the base model. 

				
					

				
			
You can hang HomeView on a wall, but it’ll cost extra for a mount and power adapter.

Foundry




For the tabletop model, $299 feels fair if you live in Apple’s world. You’re getting a great speaker, a gorgeous screen, a decent FaceTime camera, Siri AI, and both a shared and a personalised hub that will look great in any room. It’s also the cheapest way to access Siri AI. There are some things to consider, such as support for existing smart home products you have and whether you mind the lack of a privacy switch. I’ll need to test it fully to see how it responds to my world and my family, but from what I’ve seen so far, HomeView seems set to slot right into my home.
Apple’s HomeView arrives on November 13, and preorders are open now on Apple.com, Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers.

title: HomePod mini 2: Everything you need to know release date, price & specs
content:
Macworld





Apple has unveiled the HomePod mini 2, the first major update to its smallest smart speaker since the original launched in November 2020. Announced on October 13, 2026, the new HomePod mini brings Apple’s more capable Siri AI assistant, upgraded audio experiences, improved connectivity, and a selection of new colors. It retains the familiar compact, spherical design but features significantly improved technology inside.
The biggest upgrade is Siri AI, which will bring more natural conversations, broader knowledge, and greater awareness of personal information stored on connected Apple devices. This will allow users to ask more complex questions, find information in messages and emails, and perform tasks across apps. Siri AI will arrive in a future software update. To enable it, the owner of the home in the Home app needs an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad with current software and Siri AI enabled in a supported language. Other household members can then use its general conversational features without their own compatible device, but personal-context requests require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled device.
Apple has also replaced the original HomePod mini’s aging S5 processor with the newer S10 chip, enabling enhanced computational audio. Other major additions include four-speaker surround sound when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, the ability to use HomePod mini 2 as the default audio output for a Mac equipped with Wi-Fi 6E or later, and Sound Glow, which turns the illuminated touch surface into a colorful display that responds to music. Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6 bring the speaker’s wireless technology up to date.
The HomePod mini 2 comes in five colors: pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. It costs $149, compared with the previous model’s $129 price following Apple’s June 2026 price increase. Pre-orders opened on October 13, with the new speaker going on sale on Friday, October 30. It’s a substantial upgrade for anyone buying their first HomePod mini, although existing owners may find the strongest reason to upgrade is the new Siri experience.
HomePod mini 2 vs. HomePod mini: The 10 biggest changes


FeatureHomePod mini 2 (2026)HomePod mini (2020)

1. ProcessorApple S10Apple S5
2. SiriSiri AI, arriving laterOriginal Siri features
3. Personal contextCross-app personal context with compatible iPhone/iPadLimited personal requests
4. Home theaterFour-speaker surround sound with Apple TV 4K (4th gen)Stereo pairing
5. Mac audioDefault audio output on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E or later; supports one speaker or a stereo pairAirPlay audio
6. Visual effectsNew Sound Glow music animationsIlluminated Siri/touch surface
7. Wi-FiWi-Fi 6EWi-Fi 4 (802.11n)
8. BluetoothBluetooth 6Bluetooth 5.0
9. ColorsMidnight, white, blue, green, pinkMidnight, white, blue, yellow, orange
10. Price$149$99 at launch; $129 most recently

 



The biggest improvements are in software intelligence, audio capabilities, and wireless connectivity rather than the speaker’s physical design. Its fundamental audio hardware remains familiar, including the full-range driver, dual passive radiators, and 360-degree acoustic waveguide. 


HomePod mini 2 release date: When will it go on sale?
Apple announced the HomePod mini 2 on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at its “Welcome Home” product launch. The new speaker is available to pre-order immediately, with the official release date set for Friday, October 30, 2026.
Customers in the U.S. and more than 23 other countries and regions can order the HomePod mini 2 through the Apple online store or Apple Store app. It will also be available in Apple retail stores from October 30. Other retailers are expected to stock the speaker.
The new model arrives almost six years after the original HomePod mini launched in November 2020. Apple had been widely expected to update the speaker in 2025, but reports suggested that development of its redesigned Siri assistant delayed the launch. Standard smart-home controls will be available at launch, but Siri AI will arrive in a later software update. To enable it, the home owner will need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.
$149 at  Apple						
					
Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.S.
Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.K.


							


HomePod mini 2 design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			The Pink HomePod mini

Apple




Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the HomePod mini for its second generation. The new speaker retains the familiar spherical shape, with a seamless acoustic mesh covering its body and an illuminated touch-sensitive surface on top. It’s designed to fit unobtrusively on a desk, bookshelf, kitchen counter, or bedside table.
The HomePod mini 2 measures 3.3 inches (84.3mm) high and 3.9 inches (97.9mm) wide, exactly the same dimensions as its predecessor. It weighs 335g, making it slightly lighter than the original 345g model. Apple continues to use acoustically transparent fabric, allowing sound to travel through the enclosure in every direction.
The most obvious visual changes are the colors. HomePod mini 2 is available in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. Pink and green replace the outgoing orange and yellow options, while blue has a darker appearance than before. Interestingly, these colors closely match those revealed in Apple software before the announcement, although a previously rumored red version hasn’t appeared.
The other significant visual upgrade is Sound Glow, which makes the illuminated surface on top much more expressive. Rather than simply displaying Siri’s familiar animations, it can pulse and glow in response to the bass and treble of music. Colors can reflect the artwork of the song being played, while soundscapes such as rain produce their own lighting effects. Voice control element of Sound Glow requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running the latest software.
Apple hasn’t changed the basic touch controls. Users can still tap to play or pause music, double-tap to skip forward, triple-tap to skip backward, touch and hold to activate Siri, and use the illuminated plus and minus controls to adjust volume. The biggest interface improvements therefore come from Sound Glow and the forthcoming Siri AI features rather than new physical buttons.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 processor: What chip does it use?
The HomePod mini 2 uses Apple’s S10 chip, replacing the original model’s S5. It powers computational audio that adjusts the sound in real time, including its dynamic range and loudness.
The new model also supports the forthcoming Siri AI features, including more conversational requests and access to personal context. These will arrive through a future software update and require compatible Apple devices.
The redesigned Siri will support more conversational requests, broader world knowledge, and personal context awareness, with processing distributed between the HomePod, connected Apple devices, and Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 connectivity: What’s changed?

				
					

				
			Top of the HomePod mini

Apple




The HomePod mini 2 brings two confirmed wireless upgrades: Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6. These replace the original model’s older Wi-Fi 4 and Bluetooth 5.0 technologies, bringing the speaker up to date with Apple’s latest wireless ecosystem.
Wi-Fi 6E adds access to the 6GHz wireless band when used with a compatible router, potentially reducing congestion and improving network performance in busy homes. Bluetooth 6 introduces newer wireless capabilities, although Apple hasn’t specified which Bluetooth improvements the HomePod mini 2 takes advantage of.
The new HomePod mini also supports Thread networking, allowing it to act as part of a compatible smart-home network. This helps it communicate with devices such as smart lights, sensors, and other supported accessories without relying exclusively on traditional Wi-Fi connections.
Apple lists an Ultra Wideband chip for device proximity, continuing support for proximity-based interactions with compatible devices. However, the technical specifications don’t identify the generation of the chip, so it isn’t yet possible to confirm whether this is an improvement over the original model’s U1 hardware.
Despite earlier rumors about Apple’s in-house wireless networking technology, the company hasn’t named a specific Apple-designed connectivity chip for the HomePod mini 2. The speaker continues to depend on Wi-Fi for its internet connection.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 speaker setup
You can use HomePod mini 2 on its own, pair two for stereo sound, or build a four-speaker surround system with a compatible Apple TV – while supported Macs can use a single speaker or stereo pair.
Can you use HomePod mini 2 speakers for stereo or surround sound?
You can use one HomePod mini 2 on its own or combine two into a stereo pair, with separate left and right audio channels. Stereo pairing was available on the original HomePod mini.
The new addition is four-speaker surround sound with an Apple TV 4K (4th generation) running the latest software. This uses two speakers at the front and two at the rear.
Each pair must contain matching models, but the front and rear pairs can differ. For example, you can use two HomePod (2nd generation) speakers at the front and two HomePod mini 2 speakers at the rear.
Which Macs can use HomePod mini 2 as their default speaker?
HomePod mini 2 can serve as the default audio output for a Mac with Wi-Fi 6E or later. You can use one speaker or two HomePod mini 2 speakers configured as a stereo pair. Four-speaker surround sound requires an Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and isn’t supported through this Mac feature.
Compatible models include:
Mac mini: M2 and M2 Pro models or newer
MacBook Pro: 14-inch and 16-inch models introduced in 2023 or later
Mac Studio: M2 Max and M2 Ultra models or newer
Mac Pro: M2 Ultra model
iMac: M3 models or newer
MacBook Air: M3 models or newer


						

							


HomePod mini 2 price: How much does it cost?
The HomePod mini 2 costs $149/£149, making it $20/£20 more expensive than the previous-generation model at its most recent official price. It’s also $50/£50 more expensive than the original HomePod mini was when it launched in November 2020.
Apple initially sold the HomePod mini for $99/£99, but increased the price to $129/£129 in June 2026. The new model therefore represents another price increase, although it brings a significantly newer processor, support for Siri AI, improved connectivity, and additional audio capabilities.
A 20W power adapter is included in both the U.S. and U.K. boxes. Apple lists an iPhone or iPad running the latest iOS or iPadOS, plus Wi-Fi internet access, as requirements for using the speaker.


						

							






ModelU.S. priceUK price

HomePod mini (2020 launch)$99£99
HomePod mini (June 2026 price)$129£129
HomePod mini 2 (October 2026)$149£149
Increase over previous price+$20+£20
Increase over launch price+$50+£50

 






Should you buy a HomePod mini 2?
The HomePod mini 2 looks like a worthwhile purchase for anyone looking for an affordable Apple smart speaker, particularly those interested in Siri AI, smart-home control, new Mac audio and home theater options. The S10 chip, upgraded connectivity, and new audio features make it a much more capable device than its predecessor.
However, existing HomePod mini owners shouldn’t rush to upgrade. The design and fundamental speaker hardware remain largely unchanged, and Siri AI won’t arrive until a future software update. If you mainly use your HomePod for music, an inexpensive first-generation model could still be a good choice. For more powerful sound, consider the full-size HomePod.

title: Apple's Wall-Mounted HomeView Ships Without a Power Adapter
content:
Apple's wall-mounted HomeView will ship without a power adapter, USB-C cable, or mount, requiring customers to purchase compatible accessories separately.


In a support document posted on October 14, Apple outlined different power requirements for the two versions of its new smart home hub. The tabletop HomeView requires a USB-C power adapter rated for at least 30W, supporting an output of 15V at 2A or higher. The wall-mounted model requires at least 20W, with support for 9V at 2.22A or higher.

The tabletop model includes a 30W power adapter and a 1.5-meter USB-C cable. The wall-mounted version's box contains only the device and documentation.

Customers choosing the wall-mounted HomeView will need a compatible third-party mount and power solution. Depending on the mount, the device can use a separate USB-C cable and power adapter or a hardwired connection to line power.

If the power requirements are not met, HomeView will display a "Power Adapter Not Supported" message, accompanied by a lightning bolt and yellow warning triangle. For a wall-mounted unit, Apple suggests testing the device outside its mount with a compatible USB-C cable and adapter. If it works when connected directly, customers should contact the mount manufacturer or their professional installer.

title: Best iPhone 18 cases for iPhone 18 Pro & 18 Pro Max
content:
Macworld





You waited months for Apple’s new iPhones to arrive, but it’s worth protecting that big investment from day one. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are tougher than previous generations, but they can still be scratched, chipped or damaged in a drop. A good case also does more than protect your phone: it can improve grip, add a stand or wallet, support MagSafe accessories and give your iPhone a completely different look.
There are thousands of iPhone cases to choose from, ranging from inexpensive silicone shells to rugged cases built for serious drop protection. Price isn’t always a reliable guide to quality, either: a cheap case can split, yellow or develop faulty buttons, while spending more doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the best case for your needs.
That’s why we hand-test and compare as many iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cases as we can. We consider protection, materials, build quality, grip, raised screen and camera edges, MagSafe compatibility, weight, useful extras such as stands and card storage, and how the case feels in everyday use. Where manufacturers make specific drop-protection claims, we include those too so you can compare different levels of protection.
In this guide we’ve grouped our recommendations into clear, colorful, protective and leather or faux-leather cases, with options at a range of prices.

Which type of iPhone case to choose
Apple gives you a handful of finishes; a case gives you thousands—an easy way to make an iPhone 18 Pro look like yours. You can choose a clear case that shows off the iPhone’s original color but adds vital protection, or choose a case with more personality. Protection is key, and some cases will add higher levels of defense than others.
Beyond looks, think about how you use your phone. Want hands-free video? Look for a case with a built-in stand. Want to leave your wallet at home? Choose one with a card storage wallet. And if you charge wirelessly, check for MagSafe compatibility — most cases now offer it, and it’s worth confirming before you buy.


						

							




Best clear cases for iPhone 18
If you want to keep your iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max looking like Apple intended you could leave it unprotected without a case, or simply choose a clear case that shows off the iPhone’s color while protecting it from everyday knocks and drops.

Best protective cases for iPhone 18
As pretty as some iPhone cases are, your principal consideration should be protection. Most decent cases offer reasonable protection, but these protective cases have extra robust features while often adding as little bulk as possible by using the latest, strongest materials. Kevlar is the material used to make bulletproof vests—it’s also known as Aramid Fiber—but I wouldn’t try turning a rifle on it. Graphene is even stronger, and would probably make Superman wince trying to snap it in half.
Other protective iPhone cases don’t worry so much about thinness, and bulk up to protect your iPhone from the worst disasters that can befall it. These might suit you if you work in riskier environments or are an active outdoors iPhone user.
Material matters too: Graphene (elastic yet harder than diamond and up to 200x stronger than steel, according to case makers) or Kevlar (the material used to make bulletproof vests) for serious durability. Kevlar is a type of Aramid Fiber, a strong, heat-resistant synthetic material that gives the material incredible strength and stability.
